claim: 14 CFR 139.325(e) requires the airport emergency plan to contain procedures for notifying facilities, agencies, and personnel with plan responsibilities of the location of an aircraft accident, the number of persons involved, and any other information necessary to carry out their responsibilities as soon as that information becomes available.
source_title: 14 CFR 139.325 — Airport emergency plan
supporting_excerpt: Procedures for notifying the facilities, agencies, and personnel who have responsibilities under the plan of the location of an aircraft accident, the number of persons involved in that accident, or any other information necessary to carry out their responsibilities, as soon as that information becomes available.
caveat: Cited from the eCFR current version; subsection lettering is stable but readers should confirm against the live eCFR text at time of use.

claim: FAA Advisory Circular 150/5200-31C incorporates the National Incident Management System (NIMS) and Incident Command System (ICS) into the Airport Emergency Plan framework and organizes the AEP around hazard-specific and functional annexes.
source_title: AC 150/5200-31C, Airport Emergency Plan (Change 1)
page_or_section: Front matter and Chapter 1 (purpose and organization)
supporting_excerpt: This advisory circular... provides guidance to airport operators in the development and implementation of an Airport Emergency Plan (AEP)... The application of NIMS and ICS has been institutionalized and incorporated by reference.
caveat: Consolidated AC includes Change 2; researchers should quote from the current consolidated PDF, not older versions.

claim: FAA Part 139 CertAlert 24-09 (Oct 15, 2024) directs certificated airport operators to ensure their approved Airport Emergency Plan covers general support, communication, and notification requirements specific to sabotage, hijack, and other unlawful interference incidents, and to coordinate with law enforcement, the FBI, TSA, and other agencies identified in the AEP and the 49 CFR Part 1542 Airport Security Plan.
source_title: FAA Part 139 CertAlert 24-09: Airport Emergency Plan, Sabotage, Hijack Incidents, and Other Unlawful Interference with Operations and Aircraft Rescue and Firefighting: Operational Requirements
supporting_excerpt: Certificated airport operators should ensure that their approved Airport Emergency Plan covers the general support, communication, and notification requirements specific to sabotage, hijack and other unlawful interference incidents.

claim: ACRP Research Report 175 provides design guidelines to improve public-address systems for airport terminal environments, including background-noise data, terminal-finish considerations, and system-design principles for both new terminals and retrofits.
source_title: ACRP Research Report 175 — Improving Intelligibility of Airport Terminal Public Address Systems
page_or_section: Overview and Chapter 7 (Public Address System Design)
supporting_excerpt: The guidelines include a summary of data on public address systems, terminal finishes and background noise levels in a variety of airport terminals, identification of acoustical shortcomings, and the results of impacts on existing public address systems.

claim: ACRP Synthesis 115 gathers airport emergency-plan practices across US airports and includes case studies from Charlotte Douglas International, George Bush Intercontinental, Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International, McCarran International, Seattle-Tacoma International, Boulder City Municipal, and Centennial airports.
source_title: ACRP Synthesis 115 — Practices in Airport Emergency Plans
supporting_excerpt: Practices in Airport Emergency Plans... gathers relevant data specific to AEP practices... case studies from seven airports highlighting their successful practices and lessons learned.

claim: ACRP Report 93 addresses operational and business continuity planning for prolonged airport disruptions.
source_title: ACRP Report 93 — Operational and Business Continuity Planning for Prolonged Airport Disruptions (Final Report)
supporting_excerpt: Operational and Business Continuity Planning for Prolonged Airport Disruptions

claim: NFPA 72 requires voice intelligibility for emergency communications systems consistent with a Speech Transmission Index (STI) minimum of approximately 0.70, and references the Common Intelligibility Scale (CIS) with a corresponding minimum of 0.45 (‘Fair’) at all occupant locations within each identified Acoustically Distinguishable Space (ADS).
source_title: Mass Notification: Intelligibility is NOT Optional (Commercial Integrator)
supporting_excerpt: NFPA 72... requires a 0.70 Speech Transmission Index [STI] minimum so that a message is intelligible and therefore understood... NFPA 72 requires a minimum intelligibility rating consistent with STI of 0.45 or higher (Fair on the CIS scale) at all occupant locations.
data_vintage: reflects NFPA 72 editions in force at publication
airport_or_entity: NFPA (US code body); applicable to any NFPA-72 adopting jurisdiction
caveat: Secondary source summarizing paywalled NFPA 72; final MWAA citation should be to the current NFPA 72 edition itself, whose Chapter 24 (Emergency Communications Systems) is the primary text.

claim: NFPA 72 Chapter 24 (Emergency Communications Systems) is the chapter that governs voice-messaging and mass-notification system design, including the Acoustically Distinguishable Space (ADS) framework used to define intelligibility zones.
source_title: NFPA 72 Chapter 24 Emergency Communications Systems (ECS) — training deck reproducing chapter scope
supporting_excerpt: NFPA 72 Chapter 24 Emergency Communications Systems (ECS) 24.1 Application.
caveat: Secondary; the primary source is the current NFPA 72 edition, which is paywalled. Cited here only to fix the location of the ECS/ADS material within the standard.

claim: On January 6, 2017, a lone gunman fired a firearm inside the baggage-claim area at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport, killing five and wounding six; approximately 90 minutes after the initial incident, speculation of additional gunfire in other areas of the airport caused an uncontrolled self-evacuation of passengers, tenants, and airport employees, many of whom ran into secured areas and onto active aprons.
source_title: Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport Active Shooter Incident and Post-Event Response After-Action Report (Broward County Aviation Department)
supporting_excerpt: Passengers, tenants, and airport employees triggered uncontrolled and unmanaged self-evacuation of personnel, many of whom ran into secured areas and onto active aprons. Because of the incurrence into secure zones, the FAA issued a ground stop notice closing FLL to all but emergency flights.
caveat: AAR is the airport-authority document; the parallel Broward Sheriff's Office AAR covers law-enforcement response and self-deployment issues.

claim: The FLL 2017 corrective-action set publicly identified by Broward County Aviation Department included communications-system improvements, relocation of the emergency operations center, revised response procedures for key personnel, and enhanced active-shooter training for airport employees.
source_title: Fort Lauderdale Int'l Shares Lessons Learned From 2017 Active Shooter Tragedy (Airport Improvement)
page_or_section: Body of article summarizing BCAD lessons learned
supporting_excerpt: Communications systems improvements were among the specific projects identified, along with relocating the emergency operations center and revising response procedures for key personnel, as well as enhancing existing active shooter training for airport employees.
caveat: Trade press summary; underlying BCAD documents are the primary source and should be sought for direct MWAA-facing citation.

claim: The December 17, 2017 Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport power outage lasted approximately 11 hours; the cause was a fire in an underground electrical facility, and the redundant back-up power system also failed as a result of the same fire; the outage affected approximately 30,000 travelers and led to more than 1,000 flight cancellations on the day of the outage.
source_title: Atlanta Airport: Hartsfield-Jackson International trying to get back to normal after 11-hour power outage caused 'chaos' (CBS News)
supporting_excerpt: The power outage was caused by a fire in an underground electrical facility, which also caused the redundant back-up power system to fail... an estimated 30,000 travelers... more than 1,000 flights in and out of Atlanta were cancelled on the day of the outage alone.
airport_or_entity: Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL) / Georgia Power
caveat: News reporting; the definitive causal detail (switchgear identification and fire zone) was later attributed to Georgia Power's post-event review, not a public airport AAR.

claim: Following the January 6, 2017 FLL active-shooter event, the FAA issued a ground-stop notice closing FLL to all but emergency flights after passengers self-evacuated into secure areas including active aprons.
source_title: Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport Active Shooter Incident AAR (Broward County Aviation Department)
supporting_excerpt: Because of the incurrence into secure zones, the FAA issued a ground stop notice closing FLL to all but emergency flights.

claim: The July 19, 2024 CrowdStrike faulty software update crashed Windows endpoints globally; Delta Air Lines canceled over 7,000 flights over the following days, affecting approximately 1.3 million passengers, and airports resorted to manual operations including hand-written boarding passes in several jurisdictions.
source_title: 2024 Delta Air Lines disruption (Wikipedia)
supporting_excerpt: Over 7,000 Delta flights were cancelled affecting plans of 1.3 million passengers... While other airlines quickly recovered operations, Delta Air Lines did not.
airport_or_entity: Delta Air Lines / global airports affected
caveat: Tertiary reference; final publication should cite DOT enforcement action against Delta and Delta's own public statements as primary sources.

claim: Orlando International Airport (MCO) ceased commercial operations at 10:30 a.m. on September 28, 2022 in advance of Hurricane Ian, activated its emergency operations center, released non-essential employees, explicitly stated the airport was not set up to serve as a shelter, and conditioned reopening on sustained winds falling below 40 mph.
source_title: Orlando International Airport (MCO) Announces Closure Ahead of Hurricane Ian (BlogMickey)
supporting_excerpt: Commercial operations at MCO will cease at 10:30 a.m. Wednesday, 09/28/22... normal airport operations to resume only after the storm had safely passed and after sustained winds in the area decreased to less than 40 miles per hour.
caveat: Blog summary of official MCO operational update; the underlying MCO/GOAA press release is the primary source.

claim: The January 29, 2025 midair collision between PSA Airlines Flight 5342 (Bombardier CRJ700 operated for American Airlines) and a US Army Sikorsky UH-60L helicopter over the Potomac River near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport killed all 67 aboard both aircraft; more than 500 personnel were involved in the response; emergency officials treated on-site family care and reunification, and first-responder trauma care, as immediate response functions.
source_title: DCA midair collision first responders, others remembered by victims' families as heroes (CNN)
supporting_excerpt: Emergency officials prioritized taking care of families at the airport and making efforts to reunite them with their loved ones, as well as caring for first responders exposed to trauma. More than 500 people were involved in working the incident.
caveat: News source; NTSB final accident report (AIR-26/02) is the primary source for the incident itself.

claim: The NTSB (Feb 2026 final report) attributed the DCA midair collision to overlapping systemic failures across the FAA, air traffic control, and military operations, rather than a single cause.
source_title: NTSB blames 'deep' systemic failures for DCA midair collision (NPR)
page_or_section: Lede and quote from NTSB chair
supporting_excerpt: NTSB Chair Jennifer Homendy noted that 'deep, underlying systemic failures — system flaws — aligned to create the conditions that led to the devastating tragedy.'
caveat: News summary of NTSB report; primary is NTSB AIR-26/02.

claim: The NTSB final report on the DCA midair collision is published as NTSB AIR-26/02, 'Midair Collision over the Potomac River — PSA Airlines Flight 5342.'
source_title: Midair Collision over the Potomac River PSA Airlines Flight 5342 — NTSB Aviation Investigation Report AIR-26/02
supporting_excerpt: Midair Collision over the Potomac River PSA Airlines Flight 5342
caveat: Cited from NTSB report bibliographic reference on ntsb.gov; researchers should quote from the report body for substantive findings, not from this bibliographic record.

claim: SFO's Quiet Airport program was launched in 2018 and rolled out through 2019 and early 2020; SFO reports the program reduced individual paging occurrences from 492 to 261 (a 47% reduction) and cumulative paging duration from 145 minutes to 58 minutes (a 60% reduction), and reduced announcements at gate seating areas by 40%, saving 90 minutes of daily announcement time terminal-wide.
source_title: Why is San Francisco Airport making terminals quieter? — Airport Industry Review
supporting_excerpt: reducing individual paging from 492 to 261 individual occurrences, whose cumulative duration went down from 145 minutes to 58 minutes, equalling a 47% reduction in occurrences and a 60% cut to duration.
units: paging occurrences per day; minutes per day; percent reduction
denominator: daily terminal-wide paging baseline (methodology not disclosed in this article)
caveat: Program-reported metrics; measurement methodology (which zones, which sampling window, whether adjusted for traffic) not disclosed in this article. Treat as reported program output, not audited compliance data.

claim: Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority maintains a seven-volume 2020 Design Manual described as a mandatory guide with the force of law on airport property, updated annually, with airport-specific supporting volumes for IAD and DCA; specifications are edited from MASTERSPEC for MWAA use.
source_title: Airport Context Packet — MWAA (IAD and DCA), §7 MWAA Design Manual and standards apparatus
supporting_excerpt: MWAA maintains a seven-volume 2020 Design Manual, plus Specifications and Estimating and Scheduling Standards, issued by the MWAA Office of Engineering. The Design Manual is described by MWAA as a mandatory guide with the force of law on the airport property, updated annually, with airport-specific supporting volumes for IAD and DCA.
caveat: Cited from the Stage-0 context packet; the packet in turn attributes this to MWAA Office of Engineering documents. Direct MWAA Design Manual citation should replace this in the final article.

claim: IAD carried approximately 29.01 million passengers in calendar year 2025, including approximately 10.53 million international passengers — an international share above 36% and one of the highest among major US airports.
source_title: Airport Context Packet — MWAA (IAD and DCA), §6 Passenger and operational context (2025)
supporting_excerpt: IAD: 29.01 million passengers, up 6.4% year-over-year; 10.53 million international passengers, roughly 36%+ international share — one of the highest international shares among major U.S. airports.
denominator: total IAD enplaned + deplaned passengers CY2025
caveat: Traffic totals from context packet; primary source is MWAA's monthly and annual traffic reports.
